description: Uma equipe de futuros engenheiros da computação da UNIFACENS!
summary: RollCrop is a free web tool that helps grain farmers in Brazil decide what to plant next and when. The farmer outlines their field on a satellite map and enters the crops they plan to grow, the soil characteristics, and the factors they consider most important. RollCrop compares the current crop rotation with two alternatives and, for each option, explains why it was suggested and presents the evidence, benefits, data gaps, and risks that need to be assessed locally. The focus is on timing: each crop should get through its most vulnerable stage before frost or weather conditions favorable to disease occur. Using NASA POWER records, RollCrop shows when these conditions occurred near the field in past growing seasons. These are historical records, not forecasts. The idea was validated by local farmers and seeks to support farmers and agronomists without replacing their work.
details:
What exactly does it do?

  1. The farmer creates a local profile using only a nickname, with no password. The data stays in the browser. The farmer then outlines the field on a satellite map. In this MVP, fields must be located in Itapeva or Itaberá. An optional exploration mode allows users to run simulations anywhere in Brazil.
  2. The farmer enters the summer and second-season crops, answers three questions about the soil (with an “I don’t know” option), and ranks four priorities: soil protection, water conservation, income generation, and keeping costs low.
  3. Each plan includes a detailed panel that explains why it was suggested, what the observed data show, the expected benefits, the risks that need to be assessed locally, and the remaining uncertainties.

How does it work?

  • Climate: Daily NASA POWER data (2015–2024) for the field’s location, at a resolution of approximately 50 km. For each growing season, we use these data to count the days with frost and calculate total rainfall in April and May.
  • Risk definitions (project estimates, subject to validation): Frost is defined as a daily minimum temperature of 3 °C or lower at a height of 2 m (Embrapa reference). A dry autumn is defined as total rainfall below 150 mm across April and May. For typical crop cycles, the sensitive period is 60–110 days after planting for corn and 45–75 days for soybeans.
  • Planting windows: For each possible planting date, we calculate the proportion of past growing seasons in which the event occurred during the crop’s sensitive period. Up to 10% is classified as “recommended,” more than 10% and up to 30% as “risky,” and above 30% as “avoid.” Results are displayed as “N of the past 10 years” and always refer to historical records, not forecasts. For soybeans, we use September 1 through December 31 as an estimated window based on the legally established planting calendar.
  • Soil: SoilGrids 2.0 data (ISRIC, 250 m resolution) are used only when the farmer answers “I don’t know,” and are assigned a lower confidence level.
  • Map: Esri satellite imagery is combined with NASA GIBS layers: MODIS NDVI (250 m) and SMAP soil moisture (9 km, for regional context only).
  • Costs: IBGE municipal yield and price data (PAM), CONAB production cost data, and food price data (IPCA) are combined with dry years identified using NASA POWER data.
  • Field location verification: Field locations are checked against the municipal boundaries of Itaberá and Itapeva (IBGE data) in both the front end and the back end. In exploration mode, the system never uses preloaded demo data.

What benefits does it have?

  • Prioritizes planting timing: It considers not only what to plant but also when to plant it, so the crop’s most vulnerable stage can avoid frost and weather conditions favorable to disease.
  • Shows the evidence and its limitations: Each data point identifies its source and scope—field-level data, regional data, an estimate, or agronomic knowledge—along with its confidence level.
  • Free and browser-based: The tool runs directly in the browser, and the farmer’s data stays on their own device.
  • Shows the cost of inaction: It uses benchmark prices and yields for the farmer’s municipality.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want rural producers in Brazil to discuss planting data and crop rotation options with their agronomists—relying on the same evidence—before purchasing seeds.

Next steps

RollCrop is a working MVP for two towns, Itaberá and Itapeva (SP). These are the steps to turn it into a tool farmers can trust:

  1. Validate with the people who’ll use it. Test RollCrop with farmers and agronomists in Itaberá and Itapeva, and with local extension services (CATI, Embrapa). Calibrate our hazard thresholds and the Good/OK/Poor ratings, which are estimates today.
  2. A sharper crop catalog. Add the region’s real winter options, such as wheat and black oats. Add disease-aware rotation rules: for example, prefer grasses before soybean where white mold is a problem.
  3. Work with the official tools, not against them. Show Brazil’s official planting-risk windows (ZARC) next to our calendar, so a plan never puts a farmer outside crop insurance or rural credit.
    • Deeper NASA data:extend our weather record from 10 years to NASA POWER’s full daily archive since 1981;
    • add GPM IMERG rainfall for heavy-rain and erosion risk;
    • use HLS 30 m imagery to read each field’s past crop sequence;
    • use SMAP for current soil moisture.
  4. Show the changing climate. Compare recent decades with older ones, then add NASA’s downscaled climate projections (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6), so farmers see how their risk is shifting, not just what it was.
  5. Reach more farmers. Build a Portuguese interface and a mobile layout for use in the field. Then expand from two towns to the whole Sudoeste Paulista and other regions of São Paulo.

Our goal: a free planning companion that lets any grain farmer see, before buying seed, how their rotation choice changes their odds, backed by NASA data and checked by their agronomist.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Languages: JavaScript, Python, HTML/CSS.
Front end: Vue 3.5, Vue Router 4.5, Vite 6, and Leaflet 1.9 (no UI framework).
Back end: Python with FastAPI, Pydantic, and requests; pytest for testing.
Hosting: Vercel (front end and back end).
Version control: GitHub.
Hardware: No specialized hardware is required.
